newsitem.title: GERMANY: D. Telekom starts Internet phone test.
newsitem.headline: D. Telekom starts Internet phone test.

text.p: Germany's Deutsche Telekom AG said on Friday it would begin a pilot programme allowing 1,000 German customers to place international calls over the Internet from regular telephones.
Phone users in five German cities would be able to dial an access phone number, enter a code and then place a call to New York, Washington, Toronto or Tokyo.

Internet telephony has been possible up to now only between people using personal computers connected to the global network. Telekom is one of the first network operators to allow Internet calls from standard phones.
In the T-NetCall pilot, selected callers in Berlin, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn Frankfurt and Munich could call a limited range of destination phone numbers overseas.
They would pay only 24 pfennigs (13 cents) per minute for the part of the call to a local Telekom access point, while most of the call would travel over the global computer network.
Telkom would cover the cost of completing the connection over phone lines in the country of destination.

The company -- which also operates T-Online, Europe's largest computer online service -- hopes to use the test to learn about the technology, costs and customer relationships of Internet calling. An actual rate for such calls could only be determined after the progamme ends.
Telekom admitted T-NetCall was likely to produce calls with poorer sound quality than most people are used to.
Sounds transmitted over existing phone networks travel as a single, unbroken stream of analog or digital signals because there is a constant connection between the parties.
To connect users over the Internet, sounds are turned into digital signals and broken up into separate packets of data that must then be reconstructed at the destination.
As a result, Internet callers often hear gaps and interference in their conversations.
"The busier the Internet, the greater the distance between packets," Telekom said.
However, future advances in the technology could make it possible to undercut prices of international calls, threatening one of the most profitable businesses for telecommunications companies.
-- Neal Boudette, Bonn Newsroom +49-228 26097150 ($ = 1.793 German Marks)
